dpa.structure: A unit within the Ministry of Justice, headed by the Registrar of Databases, rather than a separate independent statutory body. Since Amendment 13 it supervises, inspects, investigates (including criminal investigation of privacy offences) and imposes financial sanctions.
dpa.regional: No regional authorities. The State Attorney and police prosecute criminal privacy offences; sector regulators (Bank of Israel, Capital Markets Authority, Ministry of Health) apply sectoral confidentiality rules. The European Commission has recognised Israel as adequate since 2011.

law.name: Protection of Privacy Law, 5741-1981, with Amendment 13 (published 14 August 2024, in force 14 August 2025) and the Protection of Privacy (Data Security) Regulations 2017

complaint.how: Online complaint form on the PPA pages of gov.il; no fee reported. Complaints can be filed in Hebrew; availability of other languages not confirmed.
complaint.contact_controller_first: Not confirmed as a formal requirement.
complaint.deadlines: No statutory deadline for the PPA to decide complaints was found.
complaint.complainant_status: The complainant is a source of information, not a party: the PPA decides whether to open an inspection or investigation. Individual redress is pursued in the civil courts.

stages: Complaint, breach report, media report or own-initiative audit (sectoral audits are common)
Administrative inspection: inspectors can demand documents and system logs and enter premises; in serious cases a criminal investigation
Findings, and where a financial sanction is intended a notice of intent giving the controller the right to respond (procedural details not confirmed)
Decision: administrative warning, orders to remedy or stop processing, suspension of a database, financial sanction, and publication of the sanction; or referral for criminal prosecution
procedure.decision_maker: The head of the Privacy Protection Authority for administrative measures and financial sanctions; criminal courts for offences.

fines.imposed_by: regulator: since 14 August 2025 the PPA imposes financial sanctions itself, without going to court. Under Amendment 13 sanctions are calculated per violation from base amounts that vary by provision (secondary sources cite ILS 150,000 for key breaches and ILS 320,000 for some security breaches), scaled by the number of data subjects in the database and doubled for very large databases or repeat violations, with an overall ceiling reported as 5% of annual turnover. Secondary sources differ on the figures and the statute was not checked, but the PPA's published decisions show the method at work: a base of ILS 640,000 for late breach reporting on a high-security database of more than a million people (Menora, October 2026), ILS 40,000 for each of two documentation breaches at a municipality (Beit Shemesh) and ILS 20,000 for an incomplete collection notice (Karting), each then reduced for mitigating factors such as a clean record. Before Amendment 13 the PPA could only impose small fines (around ILS 10,000 to 25,000).
fines.public_bodies: Public bodies are within the regime and must appoint data protection officers. Local authorities can be sanctioned: the PPA imposed ILS 64,000 on the Beit Shemesh Municipality in September 2026. No sanction on a government ministry has been published; the Ministry of Education finding of October 2026 carried none, but its supervision ran under the powers in force before Amendment 13.
fines.quirks: Criminal offences: wilful infringement of privacy under s 5 carries up to 5 years imprisonment, and Amendment 13 raised database offences (such as unauthorised processing, misleading the PPA or obstructing an investigation) to up to 3 years (secondary sources). The PPA reduces sanctions for the circumstances set out in the Fifth Schedule to the Law; the Menora decision itemises them in full: 20% for no violations in five years, 30% for ending the breach on its own initiative and reporting it, and 10% for having appointed a DPO.

appeal.court: Magistrates' Court, according to a 2026 practice guide (not confirmed from the statute).
appeal.deadline: 45 days, according to a 2026 practice guide (not confirmed from the statute).
appeal.suspensive: No, unless the head of the PPA agrees or the court orders a stay, according to a 2026 practice guide (not confirmed from the statute).
appeal.further: Not confirmed. Administrative decisions of government bodies can also be challenged before the Supreme Court sitting as High Court of Justice or the administrative affairs courts, depending on the matter.
appeal.inaction: Not confirmed; a complainant would rely on general administrative law petitions, but no specific route was found.

private.courts: Yes. Infringement of privacy is a civil wrong under the Protection of Privacy Law (s 4), actionable in the Magistrates' or District Courts depending on value, and individuals can sue without going to the PPA.
private.damages: Statutory compensation without proof of harm: for general privacy infringements under s 29A, reported as up to about ILS 50,000 (index-linked, around ILS 65,000) and doubled where the infringement was intended to harm, giving the ILS 100,000 figure cited by some sources; Amendment 13 added statutory damages of up to ILS 10,000 for certain database breaches such as failure to notify or correct data. Exact current amounts not confirmed from the statute.
private.collective: Class actions are available under the Class Actions Law 2006 and are a significant risk for breaches; representative and personal actions are both used (secondary source).

cases.title: Administrative fine on a former National Insurance employee
cases.summary: On 16 September 2025 the PPA published an administrative fine of ILS 75,000, set in August 2025, on a former National Insurance Institute employee who had run 20 queries in the Institute's databases in 2020 and 2021, 15 of them on the sensitive data of a complainant and her family, for personal reasons, in breach of s 8(b). This is the older administrative fine, not an Amendment 13 monetary sanction: the conduct predates the amendment.

cases.title: Meuhedet Health Fund: first Amendment 13 sanction
cases.summary: On 21 July 2026 the PPA imposed ILS 256,000 on the Meuhedet Health Fund, its first monetary sanction since Amendment 13 came into force, for not reporting a serious security event immediately (reg. 11(d) of the Data Security Regulations). A member told the fund in November 2025 that he could see a relative's medical file; the fault proved systemic and was reported only on 27 January 2026, about two months after the complaint. The PPA held that a preliminary report is due as soon as the event is known. The amount is after statutory reductions, which the notice does not itemise.

cases.title: Beit Shemesh Municipality: a local authority sanctioned
cases.summary: On 16 September 2026 the PPA imposed ILS 64,000 on the Beit Shemesh Municipality after a fault in its GIS system exposed welfare and medical data on about 4,600 residents. Neither breach was the fault itself: a vendor with access to the database for almost two years was not listed as a holder (reg. 2(a)(7)), and the security procedure did not govern vendors' access (reg. 15(a)(3)). The PPA rejected the argument that Amendment 13 had come into force only a week before the event, since there had been a year to prepare. The base of ILS 80,000 (40,000 per breach) was reduced by 20% for no sanctions in the previous five years.

cases.title: Menora Mivtachim Insurance: the reduction calculation in full
cases.summary: On 22 October 2026 the PPA imposed ILS 256,000 on Menora Mivtachim Insurance for reporting more than two weeks late that an insurance agent had been able to see a report on 138 policyholders of another agent (reg. 11(d)(1)). The notice publishes the calculation: a base of ILS 640,000, because the database is at high security level and holds data on more than a million people, reduced by a cumulative 60% under the Fifth Schedule to the Law (20% for no violations in five years, 30% for ending the breach on its own initiative and reporting it, 10% for having appointed a DPO). The duty to report does not wait for an internal investigation to finish.

quirks: The regulator sits inside the Ministry of Justice rather than being a separately constituted independent authority, yet Israel has held an EU adequacy decision since 2011.

Until August 2025 the regulator had almost no fining power. Amendment 13 gave it GDPR-style administrative sanctions, but the first came almost a year later: by the end of October 2026 the PPA had published four, Meuhedet (ILS 256,000, 21 July 2026), A.D. Karting Hutzot (ILS 12,000, 5 August 2026, for a registration form that took ID numbers and a child's details without the notice s 11 requires), the Beit Shemesh Municipality (ILS 64,000, 16 September 2026) and Menora Mivtachim Insurance (ILS 256,000, 22 October 2026). Two of the four are for late breach reporting.

The PPA also publishes findings of violation that carry no sanction, usually because the events predate Amendment 13: the Ministry of Education (8 October 2026, an open link that exposed data on about 21,000 special-education pupils), the Technion (26 October 2026, an intrusion not reported immediately) and four earlier findings in its 2026 administrative enforcement register.
Individuals can claim statutory compensation without proving any harm, which makes class actions attractive.
The same authority runs both administrative inspections and criminal investigations of privacy offences.
Sanctions are scaled by the number of people in the database, not only by the seriousness of the conduct.
plain: You can complain to the Privacy Protection Authority at the Ministry of Justice, which decides whether to inspect the organisation and, since August 2025, can fine it directly. Serious cases can become criminal investigations. Separately, you can sue the organisation yourself and claim fixed statutory compensation without proving you suffered harm.
confidence: medium: the in-force date, fining power and private action are well supported, and the cases, base amounts and reductions are taken from the PPA's own notices (read 2 November 2026); the statutory fine formula, the turnover ceiling, statutory damages amounts and the appeal court and deadline could not be confirmed from the statute, and secondary sources disagree on damages figures.
